---
title: "Generalization"
description: "A model's ability to perform well on relevant examples not used during training."
term: "Generalization"
letter: "G"
category: "Machine Learning"
difficulty: "Intermediate"
---

## Simple explanation

Generalization is a model's ability to make useful predictions on new
examples, rather than only reproducing patterns in the data it trained
on.

## Technical explanation

Generalization concerns performance on a target population or data
distribution beyond the finite training sample. It is assessed using
held-out data and depends on sampling, model selection, data quality,
distribution shift, and the evaluation procedure.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

A model is useful only if it performs adequately in its intended
deployment setting. Training metrics alone cannot establish
generalization, and performance may change when users, environments, or
data collection processes differ.

## How it works

Training adjusts parameters to reduce an objective on training examples.
Validation and test procedures estimate how the resulting system
performs on unseen examples. Techniques such as regularization, more
representative data, and careful model selection may improve
generalization but do not guarantee it.

## Practical example

A vision classifier trained on daylight photos should be evaluated on
images from different cameras, backgrounds, and lighting conditions if
it is expected to operate in those settings.

## Common misconceptions

- Low training error does not imply good generalization.
- A random held-out split may be misleading if examples are duplicated
  or grouped by source.
- Generalization to one test set does not guarantee performance under
  future distribution shifts.
